what_it_does: Running a large language model on a phone is limited not by the processor's speed but by how fast the phone can read the model's weights from its RAM chip — generating each word requires loading billions of numbers from memory. This paper introduces Dynamic Input Pruning (DIP), a method that skips loading most of those numbers for each token by looking at the current input and only fetching the columns of the weight matrices that actually matter, cutting memory reads by roughly half and boosting token generation speed by 40% with almost no drop in quality.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Modern language models contain large feed-forward layers with a structure called SwiGLU, which uses three large matrices (called up, gate, and down projections) to transform each input vector. To generate one token, all three matrices must be read from RAM — for a 14-billion-parameter model compressed to 4-bit precision, that is about 7 GB per token. The phone's RAM bandwidth (60 GB/s on an Apple A18) is therefore the hard ceiling on speed.

Prior work exploited the fact that older model designs using a function called ReLU (which outputs hard zeros) could skip columns associated with zero inputs. But modern models use SwiGLU, which almost never produces hard zeros — fewer than 10% of values are naturally zero, versus up to 90% in ReLU models. Existing predictors trained to guess which values will be small fail badly on SwiGLU because the pattern is much harder to learn.

How it works. DIP sidesteps the prediction problem entirely. Instead of trying to predict which output values will be small, it looks at the magnitude (absolute value) of the current input vector and keeps only the top-K largest input elements — discarding the rest as approximately unimportant. Because each input element multiplies an entire column of the weight matrices, pruning one input element lets you skip loading the corresponding column from all three matrices simultaneously. This is the key design choice: pruning on the input, not the output, makes all three matrices sparse at once with no separate predictor network.

For accuracy recovery, small LoRA adapters (low-rank correction matrices, each a tiny fraction of the original matrix size) are fine-tuned and fused into the weight columns before deployment, adding no runtime overhead.

Cache-aware variant (DIP-CA). Not all skipped columns need to be re-fetched from flash storage — some may already be sitting in the phone's RAM from previous tokens. DIP-CA adds a gentle bias: when choosing which top-K input elements to keep, it multiplies the scores for elements whose columns are not yet in RAM by a penalty factor (gamma = 0.2). This nudges the selection toward columns already cached, increasing the cache hit rate and reducing slow flash reads, while still always fetching the highest-magnitude elements regardless of cache state.

The result. On Phi-3-Medium evaluated against Apple A18 hardware parameters: 46% lower memory footprint and 40% faster token generation at less than 0.1 increase in perplexity (a measure of text quality, where lower is better) compared to loading the full dense model. DIP-CA beats even the theoretically optimal Belady cache eviction oracle when combined with a simple least-frequently-used caching policy.
